title: Opinion | A generation taught itself democracy. Nepal’s schools must finish the job - The Kathmandu Post
description: Opinion | A generation taught itself democracy. Nepal’s schools must finish the job  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
In September 2025, teenagers in school uniforms made the most powerful argument for civic education in Nepal. A leaderless generation, organised on phones and fueled by anger over corruption, joblessness and the exodus of friends for foreign labour, brought down a government in mere days. Six months later, they voted, peacefully concluding what they had started. In the March 2026 election, voters delivered a decisive mandate to a party founded only in 2022, produced the first single-party majority since 1999 , and unseated three-decade veterans, including a former prime minister who lost his own constituency.

This moment was both a vindication and an indictment. The vindication proved what students of democracy have long insisted: a republic rises or falls on the capacity of its citizens. Economists at Harvard have found that more educated societies are more likely to build democratic institutions and defend them against backsliding. Without Gen Z weighing competing claims and seeing through manipulation, the andolan would have remained a negotiated transaction. The indictment is that almost none of them learned the how of democracy in school. Fact-checking, debating, moral clarity, organising across caste, class and region were all self-taught, improvised on social media.

The generation prepared itself. The new government must not waste this moment; rather, it must prepare the next generation of voters by making civic education a national priority.

Our neglect of civics is not unique. School systems almost everywhere have been retooled around a narrower purpose: test scores, employability and preparing workers for a global economy. That work matters in a country losing thousands of its young people to foreign labour every day.

When young people are taught to solve equations but never to inquire deeply or engage with public issues, frustration has nowhere constructive to land. Nepal saw both sides during the Gen Z uprising: extraordinary courage and arson everyone now regrets. Anger is not the enemy of democracy; unchanneled anger is. The task ahead is to equip the next generation to identify corruption, inequality, a faltering economy and a warming climate, and to press for change peacefully.

Healthier democracies do not leave citizenship to chance. In Scandinavian schools, democratic values, human rights and reasoned debate run through every subject, practised through community projects and student decision-making. These countries often excel in international civics assessments. Canada’s largest province requires every high-school student to pass a course in civics . In the United States, where democratic norms are under strain, a rare alliance of left and right has launched Educating for American Democracy to rebuild the subject so students investigate rather than memorise. That repair effort is itself a warning. Three decades ago, Robert Putnam cautioned that when civic life withers, democracy hollows out from within.

Nepal does not need to adopt this wholesale. As Amartya Sen has argued, South Asia holds one of the world’s oldest traditions of public reasoning, and our assemblies of open debate long predate the word ‘democracy’ in our textbooks. A civic education built on that inheritance, drawing on the deliberative and duty-of-care strands of our Buddhist and Hindu traditions while reforming their social hierarchies, would feel familiar rather than foreign.

The numbers leave little room for delay. Nepal ranks 107th of 180 countries on the global corruption index . More than 100,000 young people took no-objection certificates to study abroad in a single year; more than 2,000 leave daily for foreign employment . Those who stay grow up on social media, where algorithms largely write their civic education. The youth bulge is either a democratic dividend or a slow-burning fuse, and education largely decides which.

Of course, civic education alone will not fix these issues. Corruption, inequality and out-migration will keep testing this democracy, and no curriculum can substitute for economic growth and honest institutions. Still, without citizens equipped to weigh evidence, tolerate disagreement and vote with knowledge, no other reform will hold.

So, what should the government do? Start with the structure. Make civic education explicit, examinable and universal, from primary school to university, never confined to one textbook chapter. Teach government systems, but also how to manage one’s emotions, examine one’s assumptions, detect misinformation, disagree without contempt and engage in communities. The age of social media and AI demands these skills but also erodes them. Then, how it is taught. A student who has run a mock election, argued the losing side of a debate and sat on a student council with real responsibility has practised democracy, not merely studied it. Teachers must be equipped and trusted to carry those habits into every classroom.

Additionally, build it inclusive by design, so that girls, Dalit, Madheshi and Janajati students, children with disabilities and young people in remote districts become co-authors of the republic rather than bystanders. And measure it honestly: We know far too little about what our citizens understand about their democracy.

title: In disaster’s wake, Nepal government allegedly rushes climate policy for COP 31 - The Kathmandu Post
description: In disaster’s wake, Nepal government allegedly rushes climate policy for COP 31  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
The Nepal government has drawn criticism over a new national climate policy, which, according to many stakeholders, was hastily drawn up after the Bhotekoshi flood and in view of the upcoming United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP 31).

Last week, the Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment circulated a new National Climate Policy–2083 draft and sought comments and recommendations from those interested in it.

Multiple stakeholders found holes in the draft policy on addressing rising temperatures, lessons learnt from the August Bhotekoshi flood, climate governance, establishing institutional mechanisms for policy implementation, monitoring, accountability, and transparency, among others.

But the government clarified that the draft was publicised for inputs and recommendations from multiple sectors. Once the deadline is over, another draft will be proposed incorporating the suggestions received.

On Wednesday, a team of stakeholders led by the Non-government Organisations Federation of Nepal met Minister for Agriculture, Forest and Environment Geeta Chaudhary, climate change department head at the ministry Maheshwor Dhakal and others to register their reservations, Arjun Bhattarai, president of the NGO federation Nepal, told the Post.

On Tuesday, the NGO federation also called an urgent consultation among civil society members, experts, Nepal SDG Forum, Federation of Community Forestry Users Nepal (FECOFUN), Oxfam and other stakeholders. They discussed the proposed policy and decided to draw the government’s attention.

But Dhakal said that in the course of drafting, the ministry had conducted a wide range of consultations with stakeholders from line ministries, provincial governments, local governments and the donor community.

It’s not true that the policy came without consultations with stakeholders, Dhakal said. “In each province, we organised a consultation process with multiple stakeholders. Each consultation drew 700 to 1,000 people. We tried to make it more inclusive, one that can reflect and represent the spirit and voices of all clusters of society.”

They, according to Bhattarai, urged the government to make the proposed climate policy timely, inclusive, participatory, rights-based, and effective. Participants emphasised that rather than rushing to finalise the policy, the government should undertake adequate and meaningful consultations with all stakeholders, including communities affected by climate change.

Participants said that, as Nepal continues to be directly affected by the impacts of climate change, the proposed policy must be practical and implementation-oriented.

According to a statement issued after the consultation, they also emphasised that the policy should comprehensively address rising temperatures in the Himalayan region, changes in glaciers and glacial lakes, irregular rainfall, floods, landslides, inundation, drought, impacts on agriculture and food security, and increasing risks to livelihoods.

“We have expressed our concerns and reservations to ministers and officials,” said Bhattarai. It looks like the government introduced the policy in a hurry on the pretext of the UN climate change conference (COP 31) being held in Turkey in the second week of November, he alleged.

On Wednesday, Dhakal received two memoranda from different stakeholders on the new draft. “We have given a deadline to furnish the grievances and we will come up with the new draft after vetting those recommendations,” he added.

Stakeholders noted that the recent Bhotekoshi flood and the resulting loss of lives, and social, economic and infrastructural damage call for greater integration of climate risk management, early warning systems, disaster preparedness, and issues ranging from relief to recovery and reconstruction within the climate policy, said the statement.

They also said the proposed policy should not be limited to emissions reduction or environmental protection. Instead, it should place climate justice, adaptation, disaster risk reduction, loss and damage, climate finance, the rights of local communities, livelihoods, gender equality, and intergenerational justice at the centre.

During the discussions, experts and representatives from various organisations and sectors—including Manish Raj Pandey, director of the National Trust for Nature Conservation; Prakash Lama of Clean Energy Nepal; and representatives of the Prakriti Resources Centre—shared their views on the positive aspects of the proposed policy and areas requiring further attention.

According to the statement, the stakeholders demanded ensuring the meaningful participation of and rights of communities affected by and vulnerable to climate change; clearly defining responsibilities for climate governance and implementation among the federal, provincial, and local levels of government; placing the concerns of women, youth, Indigenous Peoples, Dalits, marginalised groups, and vulnerable communities at the centre of the policy and giving policy priority to climate justice, loss and damage, and social justice.

Participants at the consultation said that the formulation of a policy in itself is not an achievement; what matters is its effective implementation and the positive changes it brings to the lives of affected communities. They emphasised that the policy should be finalised only after adequately incorporating the experiences and lessons learned from the Bhotekoshi flood and other recent climate-related disasters.

They also urged the government not to rush out a policy for the sake of some donors and NGOs, said Bhattarai. “We have urged the government to hold more consultations and discussions, listen to the voices of affected communities, and finalise the policy only after incorporating their suggestions.”

The stakeholders also want the policy to ensure the access of local communities and civil society to climate finance; strengthen early warning systems, disaster preparedness, and climate risk reduction; link relief, recovery, and reconstruction with long-term climate resilience; address issues related to community forestry, agriculture, water, energy, biodiversity, and livelihoods in an integrated manner; establish clear institutional mechanisms for policy implementation, monitoring and accountability; and effectively present Nepal’s actual needs and the priorities of affected communities when mobilising international climate finance and cooperation.

title: Otters Reveal Hidden River Health Secrets Along Nepal’s Karnali - Bioengineer.org
description: Otters Reveal Hidden River Health Secrets Along Nepal’s Karnali  Bioengineer.org
publisher.title: Bioengineer.org
full_article:
Along a 39-kilometre stretch of the Karnali River in western Nepal, a team of researchers has been reading the messages that smooth-coated otters leave behind. Not literal messages, but spraints: the faecal deposits that these social, group-living mustelids place at communal latrine sites scattered along the riverbanks. Those deposits, it turns out, are far more than waste. They are communication hubs, dietary records and, increasingly, early-warning signals of how one of South Asia’s most threatened river systems is coping with mounting human pressure. A new study published in Ecology and Evolution offers the first systematic look at where these vulnerable predators choose to mark their territory and what they are eating in the lower Karnali, and the results carry a warning about fishing gear that few expected.

The smooth-coated otter (Lutrogale perspicillata) is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List and as Endangered on Nepal’s National Red List of Mammals. Across its range, which stretches from the lowland rivers of the Indian subcontinent to Southeast Asia, the species has been squeezed by habitat loss, degradation of prey resources, direct persecution and illegal trade. In Nepal, the animal is recorded from the major river systems, including the Karnali, but remains sparsely distributed across the Terai lowlands and poorly documented outside a handful of surveyed stretches. Because otters sit at or near the top of the aquatic food web, changes in their distribution and diet integrate shifts across the entire riverine ecosystem, making them practical sentinels for tracking river health.

The research team, working with approval from Nepal’s Department of National Parks and Wildlife Conservation and Bardiya National Park, surveyed both banks of the lower western branch of the Karnali River below Chisapani Bridge. The stretch cuts through a Terai floodplain mosaic of braided channels, sand bars, riverine forests and grasslands that also support gharial and Gangetic river dolphins. Fieldwork ran from early January to late February 2024, deliberately timed before the monsoon so that floodwaters would not wash away the indirect signs the survey depended on. The river was divided into consecutive one-kilometre segments, and at the midpoint of each segment on both banks, the team established nested sampling plots measuring 100 metres by 10 metres.

The survey covered 70 transects in total. Latrine sites turned up at just 15 plots, roughly 21 percent of those examined, meaning that for every transect with otter evidence, about three had none. In all, the researchers documented 32 latrine sites, some inside the nested plots and others beyond them. The distances of these sites from the active river channel ranged from 13 to 1,021 metres, with a median of 200 metres. A striking pattern emerged when the team correlated spraint counts with distance from the water: the farther a latrine sat from the active channel, the more spraints it contained. The positive correlation, quantified with Spearman’s rank correlation coefficient of 0.531, suggests that otters favour marking sites where deposits are less likely to be erased by daily water-level fluctuations or shoreline wash.

Substrate mattered too. Sandy banks supported the highest and most variable spraint counts, averaging 4.75 per site, compared with means of just 2.00 at stone and mould sites. Statistical testing confirmed that spraint counts were significantly higher on sand than on stone. The finding echoes work from India’s Cauvery River system, where loose sand was a defining feature of otter sites used for grooming and territorial marking. Sand appears to offer a better grooming surface for these semi-aquatic carnivores and improves the persistence and detectability of their marks, a combination that makes sandy banks disproportionately important for otter communication along the Karnali.

To understand what drives latrine placement, the researchers measured a battery of environmental variables at each plot: bank height and slope, river velocity measured with a floating stick, river width recorded with a laser rangefinder, the presence of braided bars and retaining walls, vegetation cover, escape cover distance, proximity to settlements and graded levels of human disturbance. After screening out collinear predictors using variance inflation factors, ten variables entered a generalised linear model with a binomial error structure. Six predictors emerged as statistically significant, and all pointed in the same direction: latrine occurrence declined with increasing distance to escape cover, increasing distance from settlements, increasing river width, faster flow velocity, the presence of islands and the presence of retaining walls.

Model simplification sharpened the picture. From 176 candidate models restricted to a maximum of three predictors, two competitive models survived Akaike’s information criterion corrected for small sample size. Both contained distance to settlement and river width, each carrying the maximum summed Akaike weight of 1.00. The effect sizes were substantial. A one-standard-deviation increase in distance from settlements was associated with roughly 53 percent lower odds of latrine occurrence, while the same increase in river width corresponded to about 92 percent lower odds. In plain terms, otters mark most intensively near human settlements and along narrower, slower sections of the river, where stable marking surfaces and predictable access points between channel and bank are easiest to find.

The proximity-to-settlement result deserves careful reading. It should not be interpreted as a preference for disturbance, the authors caution, but as evidence that otter marking activity overlaps with river sections that experience fishing, foot traffic, livestock use and riverbank modification. That overlap sets the stage for conflict, and the dietary analysis supplied a dramatic confirmation of just how entangled the two species’ fortunes have become. When the researchers dissected 32 spraint samples under a binocular microscope, comparing scales and bones against reference slides prepared from fish caught in cast nets and mounted in permanent slides, fish remains appeared in nearly every sample, 31 of 32, or 96.88 percent. Crab remains appeared in 18.75 percent of samples and bird remains in a single sample, confirming the species’ predominantly piscivorous diet with opportunistic forays beyond fish.

Within the fish component, Labeo dero dominated, appearing in 65.62 percent of spraints, followed by Tor putitora at 31.25 percent. Both are locally important food fishes that communities along the Karnali harvest for subsistence, meaning otters and people are drawing on the same prey base. But the most alarming laboratory finding had nothing to do with prey at all: fishing net material was found wrapped within 15 of the 32 spraints examined. This is direct evidence that otters are regularly interacting with gill nets, most likely while removing or consuming entangled fish. Elsewhere in the species’ range, smooth-coated otters have been reported taking fish directly from nets and damaging gear, fuelling negative perceptions among fishers. Abandoned and lost nets compound the hazard, entangling and injuring wildlife long after they stop catching fish for anyone.

The study arrives at a moment of real conservation opportunity. Rajapur and Tikapur municipalities have jointly declared Nepal’s first Fish Sanctuary, covering 3.9 square kilometres in the very stretch of river the researchers surveyed, a move intended to rebuild prey populations and regulate fishing pressure. The authors argue that practical action should include reducing destructive fishing practices and the safe disposal of damaged nets, implemented through local governments in collaboration with community-based organisations and the river-dependent Tharu and Sonaha communities. Their broader message is that otter conservation cannot be confined to remote, apparently undisturbed river sections, because the animals themselves mark, forage and raise their young in the human-dominated reaches where rivers are most at risk. In the spraints of the Karnali’s otters, scientists have found both a baseline for protecting a Vulnerable species and a blunt record of the pressures bearing down on one of Nepal’s great rivers.

title: What Nepal’s Floods Reveal About Building in the Indian Himalayas - orfonline.org
description: What Nepal’s Floods Reveal About Building in the Indian Himalayas  orfonline.org
publisher.title: orfonline.org
full_article:
The floods in Nepal should serve as a warning for India. The Indian Himalayan economy — stretching nearly 2,500 kilometres across 13 states and Union Territories, housing almost 50 million people, and supporting critical hydropower, tourism and connectivity infrastructure — is becoming increasingly exposed to a changing climate. The Hindu Kush Himalayan region lost around 12 percent of its glacier area between 1990 and 2020, while the rate of ice loss has doubled since 2000. The consequences are already visible. The 2021 Chamoli disaster killed more than 200 people and damaged two hydropower projects with a combined capacity exceeding 530 MW. Two years later, the South Lhonak GLOF destroyed 13 bridges and the 1,200-MW Teesta-III project, leaving Sikkim with an estimated INR 18,555 crore in damage, more than the state’s annual budget. Without resilience built into development, Himalayan disasters risk becoming recurring crises—costing lives, livelihoods and economic growth.

Climate resilience often enters only after the fundamental choices — where to build, what to build and how much risk to accept — have already been made.

India is expanding its Himalayan infrastructure footprint just as the climatic assumptions underlying that infrastructure are becoming less reliable. Retreating glaciers, expanding glacial lakes, intense rainfall and unstable slopes are interacting in ways that historical records cannot adequately anticipate. Yet roads, bridges, tunnels and power projects expected to operate for the next 50 or 100 years continue to be planned largely on the basis of past weather and hydrological patterns. Climate resilience often enters only after the fundamental choices — where to build, what to build and how much risk to accept — have already been made.

Nepal’s experience must therefore push India to confront a more consequential question: how much of the next Himalayan disaster can be prevented, and how?

That requires three connected shifts: detecting risk, regulating exposure and pricing resilience.

First, India must judge early-warning systems by the time they buy, not the alerts they generate.

India has significantly expanded its ability to identify Himalayan hazards. The Central Water Commission (CWC) monitors 902 glacial lakes and water bodies larger than 10 hectares, while the INR 150-crore National Glacial Lake Outburst Flood Risk Mitigation Programme is strengthening monitoring and early-warning systems across four Himalayan states. However, the 2023 South Lhonak GLOF exposed the gap between identifying a hazard and translating that information into timely action. The lake had been recognised as potentially dangerous years before its outburst, yet no operational warning reached downstream communities before the flood devastated the Teesta valley. Following the disaster, the CWC identified 47 dams potentially exposed to GLOFs; as of 2024, studies had been completed for only 31.

India must build the missing link between forecast and action by institutionalising impact-based forecasting and forecast-based action protocols for high-risk

Therefore, India must build the missing link between forecast and action by institutionalising impact-based forecasting and forecast-based action protocols for high-risk Himalayan catchments. Inundation and downstream impact modelling should establish where a flood will travel, what settlements and critical infrastructure lie in its path, and the likely lead time downstream. These impact maps should be integrated into district and state disaster-management plans and linked to pre-defined warning thresholds and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) for road closures, evacuations and protection of critical infrastructure and essential services. High-altitude monitoring systems should have redundant sensors, backup power and multiple communication channels so that the hazard itself does not disable the warning system.

Second, India must price the cost of failure before building infrastructure.

India’s infrastructure appraisal largely captures construction costs, while the wider economic costs of infrastructure failure remain inadequately reflected in project decisions. In the Himalayas, these losses multiply as damaged infrastructure disrupts connectivity, electricity, tourism, supply chains and essential services. The Coalition for Disaster Resilient Infrastructure (CDRI) estimates India’s annual average infrastructure losses from disasters at nearly US$32 billion, while an additional 10–15 percent investment in resilient infrastructure design can generate economic returns of seven to twelve times through avoided losses.

India should therefore embed climate-risk screening, lifecycle costing and resilience cost-benefit analysis into Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) and public investment appraisal for major Himalayan infrastructure. Projects should account not only for capital expenditure, but for expected lifetime costs, including reconstruction, service downtime and cascading economic losses. CDRI’s existing Resilience Cost-Benefit Analysis provides a ready framework for project appraisal, financing and procurement.

These assessments must be forward-looking rather than historically calibrated. Infrastructure expected to operate until 2070 or 2080 should be stress-tested against projected changes in rainfall intensity, flood discharge, GLOF exposure and slope instability. Resilience must become an upfront investment criterion rather than a reconstruction cost after disaster strikes.

Third, India must stop creating new vulnerabilities in the Himalayas.

Climate-resilient infrastructure is not only about building stronger; sometimes it means deciding where not to build. Uttarakhand received more than six crore tourists and pilgrims in 2025, while Himachal Pradesh received 1.81 crore tourists in 2024. Pilgrimage infrastructure and commercial construction are following this growth, often into narrow valleys and constrained mountain towns where land and evacuation routes are limited. NITI Aayog has itself argued that tourism growth in the Indian Himalayan Region must be governed by local carrying capacity.

India must therefore institutionalise multi-hazard risk zonation within statutory land-use planning and Development Control Regulations (DCRs). District and urban development plans should overlay landslide susceptibility, floodplains, debris-flow channels and potential GLOF inundation zones with settlements, tourism infrastructure, transport corridors and critical services. These maps should determine what can be built and at what intensity: prohibiting new high-occupancy development in very high-risk zones, restricting density in intermediate-risk areas and directing growth towards safer locations. Carrying-capacity assessments should also incorporate evacuation capacity — not simply how many tourists a destination can accommodate, but how many people can be moved safely if a road, bridge or communication network fails.

The choice is not between development and conservation, but between infrastructure planned around historical risks and development designed to withstand the risks of tomorrow.

The institutional architecture partly exists. The National Disaster Management Authority’s (NDMA) landslide-management guidelines provide for hazard zonation and regulation of development in vulnerable areas, while floodplain zoning has long been part of India’s disaster-risk framework. The missing step is to make these assessments legally consequential for master plans, building permissions and infrastructure approvals. A hazard map that identifies vulnerability but does not alter where or how construction occurs is information, not risk reduction.

Continued infrastructure development in the Himalayas will remain important for India’s connectivity, livelihoods and economic development. The Nepal floods, however, underline the need to ensure that new infrastructure accounts for a climate that is changing rapidly. The choice is not between development and conservation, but between infrastructure planned around historical risks and development designed to withstand the risks of tomorrow.

title: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods far beyond affected areas, ILO assessment finds - International Labour Organization
description: Nepal floods threaten jobs and livelihoods far beyond affected areas, ILO assessment finds  International Labour Organization
publisher.title: International Labour Organization
full_article:
Kathmandu, (ILO news) – Catastrophic floods in Nepal have severely disrupted employment and livelihoods, with consequences extending well beyond the areas directly affected, according to a preliminary assessment released by the International Labour Organization (ILO).

On 26 August 2026, a flash flood swept down the Bhote Koshi–Trishuli corridor from the Nepal-China border resulting in major loss of life and economic damage.

The assessment estimates that around 21,400 employed people live within four kilometres of the mapped flood footprint. The destruction of homes, workplaces, roads, bridges and energy infrastructure has disrupted economic activity and workers’ ability to reach jobs, markets and essential services.

It identifies tourism, agriculture, transport and micro and small enterprises as facing significant pressures. Workers such as guides, porters, hotel and restaurant workers, transport operators and agricultural workers may face reduced earnings, interrupted work and difficulties accessing customers, inputs and markets.

Nepal’s high level of informal employment means that many workers have limited income and social protection buffers. Daily wage, casual and informal workers, own account workers and micro and home-based enterprises can therefore experience income losses quickly when economic activity is interrupted, even where jobs are not formally lost.

Damage to transport and electricity infrastructure is likely to amplify the initial shock, transmitting the effects of the flood from directly affected households and enterprises to the wider local and regional economy.

Disruption to the Nepal–China trade corridor could also affect enterprises and workers far beyond the flood-affected districts. The Rasuwa and Tatopani border crossings together accounted for around 22 per cent of Nepal’s imports from China in 2025–26, while Rasuwa – where the flood severely damaged critical transport infrastructure – handled nearly half of Nepal’s exports to China. Disruption to these trade flows could transmit employment and income effects across a range of activities. The extent of these effects will depend on the duration of the disruption, the availability and cost of alternative trade routes, and the ability of enterprises to adapt.

The assessment stresses that recovery and reconstruction can help protect livelihoods while creating decent employment. It calls for immediate income and enterprise support alongside employment-intensive reconstruction, job matching and skills development, occupational safety and health measures, stronger social protection and support for resilient enterprises.

“The employment consequences of this disaster will not stop at the edge of the flooded area. Damage to transport links, electricity infrastructure and trade routes can carry the shock through supply chains, markets and connected services, affecting workers and enterprises much farther away,” said Numan Özcan, ILO Country Director for Nepal. “Recovery must therefore protect livelihoods as well as rebuild infrastructure and use reconstruction to create decent jobs and strengthen resilience.”

publisher.title: TheUnion.com
full_article:
Join Dave Weixelman for an evening of highlights and stories from his 10-day trek to the Langtang Valley in Nepal in fall 2025. The trip provided an incredible, immersive experience in one of the most beautiful places on earth.

Highlights of his trip included visiting the city of Bhaktapur, near Kathmandu, visiting temples and palaces in Durbar Square, and trekking to villages in the high Himalayan mountains. Dave enjoyed botanizing and seeing the diverse flora in the mountains of Nepal.

He will also update us about the disastrous floods, which occurred recently on August 26. It was triggered by a massive glacier-related collapse that caused catastrophic flash flooding across multiple districts, including the area of his 2025 trek, near the village of Syabrubesi on the Bhote Koshi River area of Nepal, one of the hardest hit areas in the flooding. Donations to CATS received that evening will be donated to Nepal and Tibet relief efforts. The public is welcome to meet the presenter and enjoy cookies afterwards.

Dave obtained a B.A. in botany and an M.S. in natural resources management from the University of Alaska, Fairbanks. Now retired, he was a botanist with the U.S. Forest Service for 37 years. Dave’s hobbies include botany, astronomy, and hiking, especially in the high mountains of North America and, most recently, in Nepal.

This slideshow and presentation are part of Community Asian Theatre of the Sierra's (CATS) Cultural Enrichment Program.

For more information on CATS, visit catsweb.org.

title: What the Himalaya can learn from the Andes - Nepali Times
description: What the Himalaya can learn from the Andes  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
The Trisuli Valley flood on 26 August has led to a renewed sense of urgency in addressing Glacial Lake Outburst Flood (GLOF) risk in the Himalaya. While there were geological forces at play in the Langtang Lirung slope collapse, glacial lakes similarly present a looming danger exacerbated by rising global temperatures.

On the other side of the planet, Peruvian communities have been coping with GLOFs since the 1940s. The history of glacial risk reduction in the Andes reveals lessons about what works and what does not.

The first and perhaps most important lesson from the Andes is the importance of consistent funding and public oversight when it comes to glacial risk reduction.

In 1941, a GLOF from Lake Palcacocha in Peru’s Cordillera Blanca mountain range killed thousands of people in the city of Huaraz and motivated the Peruvian government to study and control glacial lakes. Over the years, public hydropower companies supported that work, recognising its importance to their industry.

In 1970, a debris avalanche and mudflow off Mt Huascaran, similar to what happened in Nepal last month, was triggered by an offshore earthquake and destroyed the Peruvian town of Yungay, killing 30,000 people – the deadliest glacier-related disaster in history.

By the 1990s, Peru had completed a survey of glacial lakes in the Cordilla Blanca, identified which ones were hazardous, and intervened at 34 of them. Researchers and engineers developed a suite of strategies to manage lakes, from simple channels and earthen dams to complex valve systems.

However, neoliberal reforms beginning some 25 years ago led to the dissolution of state-run agencies and the privatisation of hydropower in Peru. Projects were underfunded and stalled even while global warming exacerbated the risks posed by glacial lakes in the Andes. In 2024, Lake Palcacocha flooded Huaraz for the first time in more than 80 years.

Even as Peru’s policy infrastructure for reducing GLOF risks began to decline, scientists found ways to exchange knowledge – including through a series of three USAID-funded workshops in Nepal and Peru hosted by Alton Byers, a mountain geographer at the University of Colorado Boulder.

Peruvian and Nepali scientists at Imja glacial lake in Khumbu. Photo: SKYSHIP FILMS

Byers says it was important that the workshops did not resemble stale conferences: In 2011, 25 participants set out on a five-week trek to observe Imja Tso firsthand. One of them was Peruvian civil engineer César Augusto Portocarrero Rodríguez, who became invested in Nepal’s GLOF risk reduction efforts and would later contribute to projects like the draining of Imja Tso.

Tso Rolpa and Imja Tso were lowered by about 3m each in 2000 and 2016 respectively, and Nepal is planning similar projects on four other potentially dangerous glacial lakes with support from the Green Climate Fund (GCF): Lumding Tso, Hongu-2, Lower Barun and Thulagi.

Still, while Nepal continues to implement GLOF risk reduction strategies from Peruvian pioneers, the Andes and Himalaya are dramatically different contexts.

Byers recalls Portocarrero telling him: “The first step to controlling a lake is building a road to it.” Building a road to a glacier is a relatively straightforward task in the Andes, where mountains jut upwards from grasslands, but is much more difficult and expensive across much of the Himalaya. These limitations have meant relying on straightforward techniques, like open channels, as opposed to the more elaborate siphon systems that are common in Peru.

With Nepal demanding climate reparations to rebuild after the Trisuli Valley flood, Peru also sets an example in reallocating accountability from the places most impacted by climate breakdown to the actors causing it.

A decade before Lake Palcacocha’s 2024 flood, Peruvian farmer and mountain guide Saúl Luciano Lliuya filed a lawsuit against RWE AG. With support from Germanwatch, Lliuya argued that the German energy provider has contributed 0.47% of the emissions causing climate change and should therefore be responsible for 0.47% of the costs associated with protecting his Huaraz home.

In 2017, Lluyia won an appeal determining that major emitters can be held liable for risks resulting from climate change under German civil law. Ultimately, however, his case was dismissed. The court did not consider his home to be at high enough risk of flooding. Even though a GLOF from Lake Palcacocha would most likely inundate his property and such an event is highly likely to occur at some point, it is highly unlikely to occur in any given year.

Byers says that similarly contradictory calculations of risk account for the prevalence of ill-fated hydropower infrastructure on Nepal’s rivers. But, he adds, if an area has “been under water once from a GLOF, it will be underwater again”. Modeling and field observations – from both scientists and local elders who are intimately familiar with recurring flood patterns – can help keep this reality front-of-mind.

A mural in Huaraz depicts evacuation routes. Photo: AUDREY FROMSON FOR PULITZER CENTER

EARLY WARNING

Like experts from Nepal, Byers points to early warning systems that combine real-time lake and glacier monitoring with community-based preparedness strategies as a priority, especially post-Rasuwa.

Peru is developing early warning systems, too. Strategies include identifying which environmental variables are both critical to early detection and measurable by sensors, targeting text alerts to community leaders like school principals and hospital chiefs, and hosting workshops along the catchment area to understand how different communities perceive risk.

In Huaraz, a mural depicting evacuation routes demonstrates how embedded knowledge of GLOF risk has become in the local community.

Byers highlights the importance of participatory and place-based system design: “Every lake is different, every hanging glacier is different, and every warning system will be different.”

title: Nepal’s PM says when the house is burning, we act - The Japan Times
description: Nepal’s PM says when the house is burning, we act  The Japan Times
publisher.title: The Japan Times
full_article:
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah told the United Nations General Assembly last week that he wished he could speak simply about “development, democracy, peace and the hopes of a young nation.” Instead, he said, “I must speak about death and destruction of epic proportions.”

Nepal’s recent catastrophic flash floods, Shah said, were “not just a local tragedy, it was a warning to the world.” He emphasized that “climate change does not recognize borders. Glaciers and floods do not travel with a visa stamped on passports.” Yet global leaders have been negligent in translating those warnings into action at the speed and scale required.

Nepal has never burned much coal or drilled for oil. Nepal produces a negligible share of greenhouse gas emissions. Yet on Aug. 26, a giant torrent of water swept away villages, engulfed people and damaged roads and hydropower facilities near the Nepal-China border. The death toll from the devastating floods surpassed 1,450 and thousands are still missing. Four weeks later, Shah stood before the UNGA to deliver a stark question: Has the world truly heard this warning or simply filed it away with the rest?

title: Landslides continue in Nepal; trekkers leave routes unfinished · BNN - Baltic News Network
description: Landslides continue in Nepal; trekkers leave routes unfinished · BNN  Baltic News Network
publisher.title: Baltic News Network
full_article:
As Nepal struggles to cope with the aftermath of catastrophic flash floods in August, a new series of landslides and heavy downpours has claimed the lives of approximately 30 people, the BBC reports.

The country's disaster management center reported that since last week, rains and landslides have affected more than 1,900 families; over 240 homes have been damaged or destroyed, and buildings, bridges, and roads have been washed away. Hundreds of tourists hiking the Annapurna Circuit—a route vital to Nepal's economy—have been forced to abandon their treks and return to safety. Many have been airlifted out of the Manang and Mustang districts. Completing the Annapurna Circuit typically takes three weeks.

Speaking to the BBC beside a sodden blue tent in Batar, local resident Buti Tamang said he used to live in a small house but now has nothing left, having also lost many relatives. Ramesh Gale, who was also forced to leave his home, noted that the rain is pouring, water is seeping into the tent, and the situation is difficult. Several tourists and their guides described the descent from the mountains as perilous; the journey took three to four days and required traversing collapsed roads and washed-out bridges. Jake Stacy, a 21-year-old from Suffolk, was stranded with his guide in the upper Manang area due to snow and decided against continuing to Thorong La Pass, the highest point of the Annapurna Circuit. They made their way down steep, extremely muddy mountain slopes. He added that

many tourists were evacuated by helicopter.

Australian Andrew Graham and his guide recounted having to cross more than 15 landslides on their way back from the village of Manang, many of which were highly dangerous. They found themselves at a dead end upon reaching the village of Chame—which had been evacuated due to the risk of landslides—and were forced to spend the night in the jungle. A major landslide had blocked the river flowing through Chame, creating a lake that submerged houses and the main bridge. Authorities are attempting to drain the lake using excavators, but so far, these efforts have been unsuccessful. Trekking guide Tse Ring Dom said that she and her group had to cross 28 landslides, and—given the disaster in August—the mental stress was greater than the physical challenges.

full_article:
At least 30 people have died in Nepal following a fresh wave of heavy rain and landslides, coming shortly after devastating August flash floods killed over 1,400 people.

The severe weather has washed away crucial roads and bridges, leaving local communities cut off and forcing hundreds of trekkers to abandon their journeys.

Rescue operations were launched to airlift stranded travellers from remote Himalayan villages, including Samagaun, as well as regions such as Manang and Mustang.

An avalanche near Himlung Peak killed at least four people and left 12 missing, with search and recovery efforts temporarily suspended due to poor weather.

Authorities warned that more than half of the country faces a high risk of flooding, while power supplies and infrastructure remain severely disrupted.

State-owned operator Nepal Telecom reports it has incurred NPR 88.512 million in infrastructure damage across its mobile, wireline, and backbone transmission networks following severe flash floods in the Rasuwa, Nuwakot, and Dhading districts. title: Japan relief workers help to identify Nepal flood victims - nhk.or.jp
description: Japan relief workers help to identify Nepal flood victims  nhk.or.jp
publisher.title: nhk.or.jp
full_article:
Disaster relief teams are still hard at work in Nepal, more than a month after a landslide on the China border triggered massive flooding. The Japanese government is assisting with one of the big challenges -- victim identification.

Authorities in Nepal say the disaster on August 26 left more than 1,400 people dead, with over 5,200 others unaccounted for.

The Japanese team spent two weeks collecting fingerprints and DNA samples from recovered bodies. So far, about 110 victims have been identified and returned to their families. That accounts for less than 10 percent of those confirmed dead.

Many of the remains were badly degraded. Shinto Yasuharu, Deputy Chief of Mission of the Japanese Embassy in Nepal, said identifying the victims is extremely challenging. He added: "Nepal receives many tourists, and foreign nationals are among those still missing. We need to accelerate this process."

The Japanese government plans to provide DNA analysis equipment and dispatch additional specialists to Nepal.
